Reflecting on the November 30 Rally 

From Bonifacio to Today: A Nation Still Searching for Heroes

“A nation divided against itself cannot stand.”
This truth, timeless and unyielding, echoes through our history and reverberates in our present.

As I reflected on the November 30 rally, the date carried a heavy reminder: 128 years ago, one of our greatest heroes met his tragic end—not at the hands of foreign oppressors, but by fellow Filipinos. Andres Bonifacio, the “Father of the Philippine Revolution,” who lit the fire of independence through the Katipunan, was executed under orders from Emilio Aguinaldo. His death remains one of the most painful lessons of our past: that betrayal and ambition within can destroy even the noblest struggle for freedom.

⚔️ Magdalo vs. Magdiwang: Division in the Revolution

The Magdalo and Magdiwang factions in Cavite embodied this destructive division.

• Magdalo, led by Baldomero Aguinaldo (with Emilio Aguinaldo as its rising figure), sought to replace the Katipunan with a formal revolutionary government.
• Magdiwang, led by Mariano Álvarez, remained loyal to Bonifacio and the Katipunan system.

Their rivalry culminated in the Tejeros Convention (March 22, 1897), where Aguinaldo was elected president and Bonifacio was sidelined. Bonifacio’s protest against the results led to his arrest and eventual execution on May 10, 1897.

The timeline is stark:

• Aug 1896: Katipunan revolt begins.
• Dec 1896: Bonifacio arrives in Cavite to mediate factional disputes.
• Mar 1897: Tejeros Convention deepens division.
• May 1897: Bonifacio executed by fellow revolutionaries.
• Dec 1897: Pact of Biak-na-Bato halts the revolution temporarily.

This sequence shows how internal betrayal proved as fatal as Spanish bullets.

🔥 Echoes in the Present

That story of division is not confined to history. Today, the Philippines faces a different enemy—corruption. Our health care system falters, education stagnates, the economy limps forward, and scandals erode trust at every level of government. 

Politicians enrich themselves while ordinary citizens bear the weight of broken promises. Just as Bonifacio was betrayed by those who should have stood beside him, the Filipino people are betrayed by leaders who pledge reform but deliver only self‑interest.

The November 30 rally against corruption, coinciding with Bonifacio Day, is more than symbolic—it is a mirror. Bonifacio’s “Cry” sparked a revolution, but his execution revealed the dangers of disunity and the absence of integrity. 

Today’s rallies risk becoming cries without consequence—loud but hollow—unless they are matched with accountability, courage, and genuine leadership. Bonifacio’s fire was real; ours must be rekindled.

✨ The Call to Action

The lesson is clear: revolutions fail when true heroes are silenced or absent. The Philippines does not need more slogans or staged spectacles. We need leaders who embody honesty, competence, and sacrifice. We need results—corrupt officials jailed, institutions reformed, and governance measured by deeds, not words.

Bonifacio’s death reminds us that betrayal from within can be as destructive as oppression from without. Our present crisis of corruption is a continuation of that same struggle. Until we find and nurture true heroes—leaders who put the nation above themselves—the Philippines will remain trapped in cycles of outrage and disappointment.

In the end, Bonifacio’s story is not just history—it is prophecy. It reflects our unfinished revolution, our ongoing search for justice, and our yearning for integrity in leadership. 

The revolution he began is not over. The search for true heroes continues.

#RelentlessForChange 

Dr. Tony Leachon
